question: How should you recite in the silent prayers, and must you use tajweed and pause after every verse?
asked: What does it mean to recite silently in the silent prayers? Does one need to recite with tajweed, and is it obligatory to pause between each and every verse?
answer:
This question deals with the issue of the silent salah. As we're all aware, Dhuhr and Asr are silent salah, and obviously the last rak'ahs of Maghrib and Isha, and the sunnah and the nafl prayers; these are silent salah. Now, a lot of people misunderstand what it means that the salah is silent, and they unfortunately make a very major error, a huge error, of keeping their mouth shut and imagining Surat al-Fatiha, imagining Surat al-Ikhlas, and nothing moves. They're just standing there, and in their heads they're saying "Alhamdulillah." That is actually not a recitation.

Now, 'afa Allahu 'amma salaf: Allah has forgiven what they didn't know. But technically the salah is not valid, technically. If you didn't know, Allah is going to forgive you. But from now on, now that you've heard this response, never, ever just stand there silently when you are praying. If you're behind the imam, then there's a controversy: do you recite or not? But if you are praying on your own, **the silent prayer means that you recite in a manner that the person next to you doesn't hear.**

Now, what is the minimal level of being silent? Our scholars mention that the minimal level is that your tongue and your lips move with the pronunciation and with the expulsion of air, but so silently that even the one next to you might not hear what you are saying. So if I were to do this, you will not hear it with the microphone. Like that. I'm reciting. If somebody were standing right here, they might just hear "Rahman" and then "Maliki"; they might hear that. They cannot hear the whole thing. That is the minimal level of being silent: that air is coming out and your tongue and your mouth are verbalizing the words, but it is so soft that even a person next to you cannot hear. And even better than this, or higher than this, is that you do it basically in a whisper. That is what is meant by the silent prayer. And the jahriyyah is that you recite in a manner that people around you can hear: "Alhamdulillahi Rabbil-'Alamin."

By the way, the fact that a prayer is jahriyyah or sirriyyah, these are not arkan or wajibat. And in case you accidentally forget or whatnot, your salah is valid. So in case you recite Maghrib as sirriyyah, for example, and you're alone and you just recite "Alhamdulillahi Rabbil-'Alamin, Ar-Rahman Ar-Rahim" in a sirriyyah manner, it's against the Sunnah, but you haven't broken a wajib; you haven't done something that makes the salah null and void. But better than this, of course, is to do the jahriyyah for Maghrib and Isha and Fajr, and the sirriyyah, of course. So if accidentally you said "Alhamdulillahi Rabbil-'Alamin" out loud in Dhuhr, your salah is not batil. It's a sunnah for it to be sirriyyah and jahriyyah.

The point being that she asked the proper way, and so it must be enunciated. And we know this as well because our Prophet ﷺ would recite in Salat al-Dhuhr and Salat al-Asr, and people in the first row, if they listened carefully, could hear a phrase or two and know which surah he recited. So the fact that people in the first row, that's four feet behind, could just barely pick up what was being said illustrates that the Prophet ﷺ would recite the sirriyyah in a way that even three feet away a phrase was heard. And that's the meaning of being silent.

Now, you asked about the rules of tajweed and pausing between the verses. No, it is not obligatory to do that, and if you do not do that, your salah is completely acceptable. And pausing between the verses actually is not even something that needs to be done in the fard salah. As for tajweed, those who know tajweed must definitely utilize it in the jahriyyah salah. If you do not know the rules of tajweed, then you are exempt, or forgiven. But in the sirriyyah you do not have to perfect the rules of tajweed. Of course, if you do so, it is better for you. And you do not have to pause after every verse. You can say, "Alhamdulillahi Rabbil-'Alamin, Ar-Rahman Ar-Rahim, Maliki Yawm al-Din, Iyyaka na'budu wa iyyaka nasta'in." Of course, it's not good; you're going quickly. But the salah is still accepted and valid. And Allah 'azza wa jall knows best.
